questions.topic: Race compared with sex as grounds of classification
questions.learningObjective: Compare race and sex as grounds of classification
questions.stem: Your studio brief proposes a hiring plan that classifies candidates by race, and the partner asks how the law treats race compared with sex as grounds of classification.

options.text: Race and sex receive identical treatment, so the plan is reviewed the same way for both.
options.misconception: assumes race and sex are treated alike

options.text: Race receives the most demanding review of any classification, while sex receives a less demanding but still heightened review.
Sex receives the most demanding review, because sex classifications have historically been more common.
options.misconception: reverses the two lines of review

options.text: Neither is heightened, so both are reviewed only for whether the rule is arbitrary.
options.misconception: denies that any classification is suspect

questions.explanation: Race classifications are suspect and receive strict scrutiny; sex classifications are quasi-suspect and receive intermediate scrutiny. The difference reflects the stigmatic risk attached to race.
questions.hint: One line is stricter than the other.

options.text: Classifications that are suspect, and classifications that are pretextual.
options.misconception: pairs the wrong two lines

options.text: Classifications that burden a group, and classifications that burden a person.
options.misconception: invents a group-versus-person distinction

options.text: Classifications that are suspect or quasi-suspect, and classifications that are neither.
Classifications drawn by statute, and classifications drawn by agency rule.
options.misconception: confuses who made a rule with what the rule does

questions.explanation: The Court divides classifications into suspect grounds, quasi-suspect grounds, and ordinary grounds, and the category fixes the standard of review. Other divisions do not match the Court's.
questions.hint: The category of the ground fixes the standard.

questions.stem: How does the equal protection clause treat the height requirement described in the memo?

options.text: If the height rule is written in sex-based terms, it is a sex classification and receives intermediate scrutiny; if it is neutral, purpose must be shown.
A physical standard is never subject to heightened review, because it measures ability rather than status.
options.misconception: assumes physical standards escape the suspect category

options.text: The rule is valid unless it is proved to be based on race, because only race triggers heightened review.
options.misconception: confines heightened review to race

options.text: The rule must be struck unless the firm shows it is narrowly tailored to a compelling interest.
options.misconception: applies strict scrutiny to a physical standard

questions.explanation: A physical standard is judged by how it is drawn and applied. Express sex-based terms trigger intermediate scrutiny; a neutral standard requires proof of discriminatory purpose.
questions.hint: Look at how the rule is written, not only at its effect.

options.misconception: treats any licensing as presumptively valid

options.text: It is unconstitutional, because licensing always burdens speech.
options.misconception: assumes licensing and speech are always in tension

options.text: It is constitutional, so long as the licensing board applies the same rule to everyone.
options.misconception: confuses equal application with the validity of a prior restraint

options.text: It is suspect, because a licence that lets officials withhold a licence on their own judgment over speech invites prior restraint.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A statute punishing an argument about public business
questions.learningObjective: Explain the constitutional problem with a law aimed only at criticism
questions.stem: Explain why a statute that criminalises only a person's public criticism of a government agency's decision is dangerous, and what test a court applies to it.

answer.exemplar: A law that penalises only criticism of official action restricts speech on matters of public concern, and it is content-based because it applies because of the subject and the viewpoint. Such a law must be narrowly tailored to serve a compelling interest, and a court will not save it by calling it a regulation of disorder or of defamation when it targets only criticism.

questions.explanation: A law aimed only at criticism of official action restricts speech on matters of public concern and is content-based, so strict scrutiny applies and the government needs a compelling interest and narrow tailoring.
questions.hint: Content-based, on public concerns, strict scrutiny.

options.text: It cannot protect anyone, because federal courts apply only the federal Constitution.

It can create new rights against private parties, because state constitutions are not subject to federal limits.

The law is valid, because false statements of fact are unprotected in every setting.
options.misconception: overstates the protection for false statements

questions.explanation: The law targets the content of speech about a matter of public concern, so strict scrutiny applies and the government must show a compelling interest and narrow tailoring.
questions.hint: Content-based on a public concern, strict scrutiny.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A state constitutional guarantee broader than the federal floor
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a federal judge cannot expand federal rights with a state guarantee
questions.stem: A state guarantee of parental choice in education is broader than the federal floor, and a partner asks a federal judge to invalidate a state law under it.

options.text: The judge should do so, because state guarantees create independent federal remedies.
options.misconception: treats a state guarantee as a source of federal relief

options.text: The judge should not, because a state guarantee cannot expand the protections the federal Constitution provides.
The judge should do so if the state law is irrational, because state standards govern state law.
options.misconception: conflates federal standards with state ones

options.text: The judge should defer to the state courts on the meaning of the state guarantee.
options.misconception: turns a federal question into an appeal to state courts

questions.explanation: A state guarantee cannot be used to expand federal protections, so the federal judge cannot invalidate the state law on that basis. State courts may apply the broader guarantee within the state's own system.
questions.hint: State guarantees cannot enlarge federal protections.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A summary of an intermediate-scrutiny holding
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between the sex and race standards
questions.stem: Explain how the law treats a sex classification, and why the standard applied to sex differs from the one applied to race.

answer.exemplar: A sex-based classification is reviewed under intermediate scrutiny, which asks whether the classification is substantially related to an important governmental interest, and the government bears the burden of making that showing. A race-based classification is subject to strict scrutiny, which requires a compelling interest and narrow tailoring, because the Court has judged that race-based rules carry a stigmatic danger that sex-based rules do not.

questions.explanation: Sex classifications receive intermediate scrutiny, requiring a substantial relation to an important interest. Race classifications receive strict scrutiny, and the difference turns on stigmatic harm.
questions.hint: Middle standard for sex, strict for race.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Guarantee and standard for a racial layoff
questions.learningObjective: State the standard applied to a race-based restructuring of ranks
questions.stem: A city eliminates a rank held largely by white officers, and the plan's stated goal is a workforce matching the city's population. Counsel asks how the equal protection clause treats the plan.

options.text: The plan is subject to strict scrutiny, and the city must show a compelling interest and narrow tailoring.
The plan is subject to intermediate scrutiny, because the goal is workforce composition.
options.misconception: applies the middle standard to a racial classification

options.text: The plan is reviewed deferentially, because the city manages its own workforce.
options.misconception: treats a public employer's choices as unreviewable

options.text: The plan is valid unless someone shows discriminatory intent, because the goal is stated in neutral terms.
options.misconception: treats a racial plan as a neutral rule

questions.explanation: Eliminating a rank on the basis of race is a racial classification, so strict scrutiny applies and the city must show a compelling interest and narrow tailoring. A compositional goal does not help.
questions.hint: Race-based restructuring draws the strictest test.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Race compared with sex as grounds of classification
questions.learningObjective: State the Court's reason for drawing the race line more strictly
questions.stem: A client asks why the law draws a harder line for race than for sex, and counsel gives the reason without overstating it.

options.text: Because race differences are always larger than sex differences in the population.
options.misconception: invents a statistical reason for the legal distinction

options.text: Because race is a matter of ancestry while sex is a matter of body.
options.misconception: offers a biological framing for a legal rule

options.text: Because race is more common as a legislative criterion than sex.
options.misconception: explains the rule by legislative frequency

options.text: Because the Court has judged that racial rules carry a distinctive risk of stigma and of reinforcing prejudice.

questions.explanation: The Court's explanation is that race-based classifications carry a distinctive risk of stigma and of reinforcing prejudice, which is why the standard is stricter.
questions.hint: Stigma and prejudice, not statistics.

questions.topic: Two lines, two standards
questions.learningObjective: State the input and output of the equal protection framework
questions.stem: A brief must summarise the framework for classifying a rule for review, and the editor asks for both the input and the output.

options.text: The input is the strength of the reasons, and the output is the standard chosen to match them.
options.misconception: makes the reasons choose the standard

options.text: The input is the level of government, and the output is the standard chosen to match it.
options.misconception: makes the level of government choose the standard

options.text: The input is the nature of the ground of classification, and the output is the standard of review it attracts.
The input is the severity of the burden imposed, and the output is the standard chosen to match it.
options.misconception: makes the severity of burden choose the standard

questions.explanation: The framework runs from the ground of classification to the standard of review, and the second step follows automatically. Reasons, level of government, and severity do not select it.
questions.hint: Ground in, standard out.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A statute punishing an argument about public business
questions.learningObjective: Identify the first question in the analysis of a content-based law
questions.stem: A statute punishes only the making of a false statement about public business when made with knowledge of its falsity, and counsel explains what a court will ask first.

options.text: Whether the state has a compelling interest in protecting the reputation of its agencies.
options.misconception: begins the analysis with a compelling interest

options.text: Whether the statute is narrowly tailored to a compelling interest.
options.misconception: leads with the tailoring inquiry

options.text: Whether the statement was of public concern, which decides the case on its own.
options.misconception: treats the subject matter as the whole of the analysis

options.text: Whether the law is content-based, because punishing only one side of an argument is by definition content discrimination.

questions.explanation: The court first asks whether the law is content-based, since a law aimed at the subject and viewpoint of a message is judged by strict scrutiny.
questions.hint: Content discrimination comes first.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A licensing term with no content
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a termless licensing provision is the most dangerous in a file
questions.stem: Explain why a licensing term that says nothing about content can still be the most dangerous provision in a practice's regulatory file.

answer.exemplar: A licensing term that sets no criteria for granting or refusing permission leaves officials free to withhold it on any ground they find convenient, including grounds about the applicant's message. That is the defect the law worries about, because a system of prior restraints lets an official decide in advance that a person may not speak, and the standards that would make such a refusal reviewable are absent.

questions.explanation: A licensing term with no criteria leaves officials free to withhold permission on unstated grounds, which is the prior restraint the law forbids. Neutral subject matter does not matter; the missing standards do.
questions.hint: No criteria means unstated grounds and restraint.
